lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use opposite leaves + inferior ovary as the Dipsacales starting point, then teach two project doors inside broad Caprifoliaceae: woody honeysuckle/snowberry and herbaceous valerian.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas project-pool module across Lonicera, Symphoricarpos and current Valeriana concepts
project_scope.note: The source sheet stores Valerianella radiata and V. amarella. Current Kew places those concepts in Valeriana, so the learner uses Valeriana as the teaching genus while preserving Valerianella as source-name provenance.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start at the node: leaves are typically opposite. Then inspect the flower for a fused corolla attached above an inferior ovary. After that, choose the woody berry door or the herbaceous valerian dry-fruit door.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Broad family with shrubs, vines and herbs. Project Lonicera and Symphoricarpos are woody with opposite simple leaves; the project Valeriana concepts are annual herbs with opposite leaves.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are usually epigynous with an inferior ovary and a sympetalous corolla. Flower symmetry and stamen number vary strongly across the family, so do not force a single corolla shape on every genus.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Variable in the project pool: fleshy berry-like fruits in Lonicera and Symphoricarpos versus a dry one-seeded fruit in the valerian lineage.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Start at the stem: SIMPLE, opposite leaves often point toward the Dipsacales neighborhood. Inspect flower and fruit next: tubular/funnelform Lonicera and bell-flowered Symphoricarpos woody branches with berries versus Valeriana herb with small flowers and dry fruit. Confirm the inferior ovary on an appropriate side view; do not equate the whole family with native honeysuckles or mislabel L. japonica as native.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: real opposite leaves → inferior ovary (macro pending) → woody Lonicera white/coral/Japanese photo contrasts → woody Symphoricarpos (photo pending) → herbaceous Valeriana (photo pending) → Viburnaceae comparison
visual_lesson.intro: Start with the broad Dipsacales features: opposite leaves and an inferior ovary. Then look at real photographs of the woody Lonicera branch to learn flower stalk origin, corolla shape and fruits. The family also includes Symphoricarpos shrubs and Valeriana herbs; these don't all have long honeysuckle tubes or red berries. Lonicera examples on this card are exact-species installed photos, not anonymous stock plants.

steps.title: 1 · Opposite, simple leaves: Lonicera example
steps.look_for: A SINGLE leaf blade on either side of a shoot. This installed coral honeysuckle foliage view is a real family example; a node close-up is still required to prove paired leaf attachment.
steps.why_it_matters: Opposite leaves help you enter Dipsacales, but do not settle the family or species. Viburnaceae also often has opposite foliage.
steps.image_credit: USDA SCS / Robert H. Mohlenbrock · Public Domain · installed

steps.title: 2 · Confirm the inferior ovary
steps.look_for: Corolla and stamens inserted above an ovary embedded below the visible flower.
steps.why_it_matters: This is a high-value Dipsacales character shared with Viburnaceae.

steps.title: 3 · Woody doorway: Texas honeysuckle flowers
steps.photo_role: terminal pale corollas / Lonicera flowering branch
steps.look_for: Pale two-lipped tubular flowers on a short flowering tip. Use the open corolla and shoot architecture as a Lonicera example, not as a universal Caprifoliaceae flower plan.
steps.why_it_matters: Woody honeysuckles use fused corollas and then form fleshy berries. Other Caprifoliaceae members can look very different.

steps.title: 3a · Axillary flower pairs: introduced Japanese honeysuckle
steps.look_for: Find the little paired flower stalks originating near leaf axils, not at the very tip of the whole shoot. The flowers may be white or yellowish with age.
steps.why_it_matters: Teaches a genus-level structural difference and flags an introduced non-native encounter plant; it is not counted as a native family representative.
steps.image_credit: Cornell NY State IPM Program · CC BY 2.0 · installed

steps.title: 3b · Long narrow tubes: coral honeysuckle
steps.look_for: Long narrow trumpet-shaped corolla with relatively short lobes, in clustered blooms at the end of a shoot. This is L. sempervirens, not the entire family.
steps.why_it_matters: Compare the proportions with the shorter, open, two-lipped flowers of Texas/white honeysuckle. Exact matched ruler-scale photos remain needed.

steps.title: 3c · Red berries on native coral honeysuckle
steps.look_for: A red berry attached to an identified coral honeysuckle shoot. Texas/white honeysuckle can ALSO produce red fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows fleshy fruit on the honeysuckle branch of the family, but red berry color does not distinguish the two native comparison species.
steps.image_credit: R. A. Nonenmacher · CC BY-SA 4.0 · installed

steps.title: 3d · Blackish berries on Japanese honeysuckle
steps.look_for: A blackish ripe berry, documented on L. japonica. Compare this with the coral honeysuckle red-berry photo above.
steps.why_it_matters: A field-useful comparison for spotting non-native Japanese honeysuckle; verify the vine's flower insertion too.

steps.title: 4 · Woody door: Symphoricarpos
steps.look_for: Opposite leaves, small clustered sympetalous flowers and conspicuous white, pink or red berry-like fruits depending on species.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows a second woody Caprifoliaceae architecture beside Lonicera.

steps.title: 5 · Herb door: current Valeriana
steps.look_for: Small opposite-leaved herb with tiny clustered flowers and a dry one-seeded fruit rather than a berry.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents the learner from equating Caprifoliaceae with woody honeysuckles only.

steps.title: 6 · Taxonomy card: Valerianella → Valeriana
steps.look_for: Source Valerianella radiata → Valeriana woodsiana; source Valerianella amarella → Valeriana amarella.
steps.why_it_matters: Keeps source provenance without teaching an outdated current genus.

comparisons.title: Caprifoliaceae vs Viburnaceae
comparisons.rule: Both often have opposite leaves and inferior ovaries. Project Viburnaceae is woody with mostly small regular 5-part flowers in broad clusters and drupaceous fruit; Caprifoliaceae includes more tubular/zygomorphic honeysuckle flowers and also the herbaceous valerian dry-fruit lineage.

comparisons.title: Lonicera vs Sambucus
comparisons.rule: Both can be woody with opposite leaves and clustered flowers, but Lonicera has simple leaves and conspicuous tubular/funnelform flowers; Sambucus has pinnately compound leaves and broad flat-topped clusters of small regular flowers.

comparisons.title: Valeriana vs Viburnaceae
comparisons.rule: Current Valeriana project taxa are small herbs with dry one-seeded fruits; Sambucus and Viburnum are woody and produce drupaceous fruits.

visual_lesson.caveat: Photos currently show REAL Lonicera flowers, leaves and two fruit colors. A photographed cross-section establishing an inferior ovary, documented Symphoricarpos and Valeriana macros, and truly measured corolla/bract arrows are still missing. Do not claim white/short, red/long, or dark fruit alone as a family diagnosis; Japanese honeysuckle remains NON-NATIVE and the native pair's three-county status remains UNRESOLVED.

genera.fast_cue: woody/vining + opposite simple leaves + tubular/funnelform fused corolla + berry
opposite-leaved shrub + small clustered flowers + conspicuous berry-like fruit
small opposite-leaved herb + tiny flower clusters + dry one-seeded fruit

taxonomy_reconciliation.note: Current Kew treats both Valerianella radiata and the Valeriana radiata combination as synonyms of accepted Valeriana woodsiana.
Current Kew accepts Valeriana amarella and lists Valerianella amarella as a synonym.
